issue: Only Code Sections One and Two had been reviewed. Sections Three to Ten were assumed irrelevant to age ratings and broadcast hours.
current_resolution: CLOSED 2026-11-06, after the first answer was WRONG. I originally scoped the Code with one test - the phrase 'significant numbers of children', which is how Rules 1.27 and 4.7 key their child-audience restrictions - and concluded Sections Three and Five-Ten were out of scope. Section Three does not contain that phrase, so the test cleared it. But Rules 3.2 (hate speech) and 3.3 (abusive or derogatory treatment) are permitted 'except where it is justified by the context', and 'context' is Section Two's DEFINED term whose third factor is the TIME OF BROADCAST. So a Section Three judgment can turn on the hour. The test could not see that, so it was the wrong test, and everything it cleared was unproven rather than cleared. Added UK-HAT-001 and UK-HAT-002.
action_required: THE RIGHT TEST IS TWO DOORS, NOT ONE: (a) 'significant numbers of children may be expected to be watching' -> Rules 1.27, 4.7; (b) 'justified by the context', which imports the time-of-broadcast factor -> Sections One, Two, Three. Sections Five-Eight instead use 'editorially justified', a narrower test that does NOT import the context definition and so never turns on the hour - verified against the live Section Five page, which uses 'editorially justified' only at Rule 5.3, uses 'justified by the context' in no rule, and mentions neither children nor the watershed nor any time of day. Sections Nine and Ten govern commercial references; Section Ten does use a context test, but for programmes about commercial companies - a sponsorship question, not a content-harm question - so it is out of scope on the same reasoning that excludes the ASA/BCAP advertising codes. IN SCOPE: Sections One, Two, Three, Four. LESSON: a single lexical test is not a scoping method. Any future country should be scoped by enumerating the escape clauses, not by searching for one phrase.

issue: Is broadcast-code-full.pdf (UK-S0) a usable substitute for the per-section HTML? It is one file covering all ten sections, which is operationally attractive.
current_resolution: NO - CLOSED 2026-11-06. It is the January 2019 print edition and predates the Code in force. Ofcom's 31 Dec 2020 statement states the Code 'is now published on the Ofcom website and is no longer available in print', so no consolidated PDF has been maintained since. The Code in force covers programmes broadcast on or after 23:00 on 31 Dec 2020; the 31 Dec 2020 amendments changed the Section Three hate-speech definition and Section Nine product placement plus minor updates; and Sections One and Two were revised again on 2023-03-16 and 2024-02-19. UK-S0 demoted to optional/original_superseded.
action_required: None. But note the near-miss: an earlier version of this repo recorded UK-S0 as CONTAINING UK-S1/S2/S4 and advised fetching it to save three downloads. Following that advice would have pinned the UK rules to 2019 text and silently dropped the 2023 and 2024 revisions - the same class of error as C-09, where an outdated edition got treated as current. The lesson is that a bundle is only a shortcut if its currency is established FIRST, and 'it is a single tidy file' is exactly the kind of convenience that discourages checking.

current_resolution: PARTLY ADDRESSED, not closed. The Toofan decision (bulletin 553, 7 Sep 2026) is collected and mined, yielding four rules: a real threshold anchor (BBFC 15 with sustained graphic violence at 11:30 breaches Rule 1.3), proof from a regulator that the offence and scheduling determinations are separate, the cultural and religious calendar as an audience-composition factor that appears nowhere in the Code text, and the finding that warnings must convey SEVERITY rather than mere presence. The guidance notes added nine further rules with worked examples. 2026-11-07: the eleven decisions the guidance names have now been IDENTIFIED to the exact bulletin issue, and the reason nobody had followed them up is now clear - EVERY ONE OF THOSE CITATIONS IS A DEAD LINK. The guidance is current and its precedent URLs all point at stakeholders.ofcom.org.uk, a hostname Ofcom has retired. The documents still exist under /siteassets/.../broadcast-bulletins/archive/obb<N>/, and the filename is not derivable (obb186.pdf, issue102.pdf and bb103.pdf all occur). It is an anchor, not a scale - it says this combination at this hour breached, not where the line sits. NEXT STEP IS MECHANICAL, NOT RESEARCH: run pipeline/fetch_precedents.py from a network that is allowed to reach ofcom.org.uk, drop the PDFs in sources/originals/, then mine them. Expect roughly 15 to 25 new rules, and expect some EXISTING rows to be contradicted, which is the point. Two existing rules already appear corroborated by decision text seen in search extracts: UK-SCH-009 (the +1 service) by the Ice Road Truckers case, where History scheduled the content lawfully at 16:00 and History+1 carried the identical file an hour later into children returning from school, and UK-SCH-008 (the watershed is a ramp) by Hell's Kitchen USA, breached eleven seconds after 21:00, and by Amores Perros, where a BBFC 18 film was held unsuitable AT 21:00 on the strength of its opening scenes. That corroboration is NOT yet evidence: it comes from search snippets, not from a stored source, so it is quotable nowhere and no row cites it. Treat every judgment_based rule as routing to a human until the files are on disk and the quote check has run.

issue: The table never records WHICH CHANNELS ITS RULES APPLY TO, and the two countries use opposite systems for deciding that
affected_rows: the applicability of the whole table, though no individual rule's content
current_resolution: OPEN, found 2026-11-07 while writing Task 2. Before you can apply a country's rules you must know whose rules apply to a given channel, and the two countries here answer that OPPOSITELY. France is in the EU and so under the AVMSD country-of-origin rule: a channel follows the rules of the country where the company is established, and receiving countries must accept that. The UK LEFT the EU, is treated as a third country under the AVMSD, and moved to COUNTRY OF DESTINATION: a service available in the UK generally needs an Ofcom licence wherever the company sits. The UK remains party to the Council of Europe ECTT, which restores an origin-style arrangement with its members but does NOT cover video on demand or IP-delivered linear TV, and seven EU states never joined it (Belgium, Denmark, Greece, Ireland, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Sweden). Work to update the ECTT was abandoned, so those gaps are permanent.
action_required: THIS DOES NOT INVALIDATE ANY ROW. Every rule in the table is about content and timing, not about who regulates whom, so the rules remain correct for channels that Ofcom and Arcom do in fact regulate. What is missing is the PRECONDITION: nothing records which channels those are, and the system takes `country` as an input as though it were obvious. PARTLY ANSWERABLE OFF THE SHELF, at least in Europe: the AVMSD obliges each member state to keep a list of the services it regulates and to publish those lists in one central public database, which is MAVISE, run by the European Audiovisual Observatory. Free, updated monthly, sourced from the national regulators, covering 42 European countries plus Morocco, about 10,000 TV channels and 4,600 on-demand services, searchable by channel with a country-of-jurisdiction field and downloadable as a spreadsheet. That is close to the lookup this problem needs, though a database entry is a record and not a ruling, so it informs a lawyer rather than replacing one. It also shows how far jurisdiction drifts from where people watch: in one year 70% of Europe's cross-border channels fell under just the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Spain, and most of Luxembourg's share was down to where the satellite uplink sits. NO WORLDWIDE EQUIVALENT EXISTS. Two actions. (1) Scope: state in SCOPE.md that the table assumes the channel is already known to be regulated by Ofcom or by Arcom, and that establishing this is out of scope. (2) Design: `country` is the wrong key for a decision; the key is the RULEBOOK that applies to that channel in that territory, which is a stored fact per channel decided by a lawyer, not something derivable from the content or from where it is watched. A channel can owe duties under more than one rulebook at once, and no recorded rulebook must produce a refusal to decide rather than a guess. Sources for all of this are web research (Ofcom post-Brexit licensing guidance, the ECTT text) and are NOT in sources/originals/, so none of it may become a rule row until collected and quote-checked.
